sections.title: BIS, BCBS and the Basel accords

blocks.text: **Basel** is a city in **Switzerland** and the seat of the **Bank for International Settlements (BIS)** (older books call it the Bureau of International Settlement). The BIS fosters cooperation among central banks with the common goals of **financial stability** and common standards of banking regulation. The broad supervisory standards come from the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)**, a group of central banks hosted by the BIS. The study material mentions 27 member nations in the committee; membership has grown over time.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** - the group of central banks that frames Basel guidelines.
The set of BCBS agreements, mainly about risks to banks and the financial system.
Ensure banks hold **enough capital to meet obligations and absorb unexpected losses**.
India has accepted the Basel accords for its banking system; the RBI issues the guidelines.

blocks.title: Before the numbers
blocks.text: The BCBS was set up in 1974 by central bank governors of the G10 countries. Its first Basel Concordat (1975) dealt with the division of supervisory responsibilities among national authorities, not with capital.

blocks.title: The three risks banks face
rows: Losses on on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet positions from movements in market prices.
Losses from failed processes, people, systems or external events.

blocks.text: In **1988** the BCBS introduced a capital measurement system called the **Basel Capital Accord**, or **Basel I**. It focused almost entirely on **credit risk** and defined both **capital** and a **structure of risk weights** for banks. The idea is simple: if a bank's capital is adequate to cover the risks it has taken (for example by funding a power plant), the bank is safe.

blocks.title: Core numbers and ideas
rows: Assets weighted by their risk. An asset backed by collateral is less risky than an unsecured personal loan, so it carries a lower weight.
According to the 2024-25 study material, India adopted Basel I guidelines in 1999.

blocks.title: Basel I in one breath
blocks.phrase: Eighty-eight, Eight, Credit: 1988, 8% of RWA, credit risk only.
letters: Minimum capital against risk weighted assets
The only major risk it covered

blocks.text: **Basel II**, published by the BCBS in **2004**, refined and reformed Basel I. It rests on three parameters, which are formally known as the **three pillars**.

blocks.title: Three parameters (pillars) of Basel II
rows: Banks keep at least 8% of risk assets as capital; in India this is the Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR).
Banks use better techniques to monitor and manage credit, market and operational risks; supervisors review them.
Banks must disclose their risk exposure to the central bank; more transparency raises trust of investors and depositors.

blocks.text: The more **transparent** a bank is, the more stable it is considered. In India the RBI publishes a **Financial Stability Report** twice a year so the system's risks are visible. The study material says Basel II norms were yet to be fully implemented in India and overseas at the time of writing.

blocks.title: Implementation in India
blocks.text: RBI moved to Basel II in phases from 31 March 2008 (foreign banks and Indian banks operating abroad) and 31 March 2009 (other banks).

blocks.title: Three pillars of Basel II: C-S-M
blocks.phrase: Capital first, Supervisors second, Market third - the CSM pillars.

sections.title: Basel III (2010): capital, leverage and liquidity

blocks.text: **Basel III** guidelines were released in **2010** in response to the **financial crisis of 2008**. They tighten capital quality and quantity, cap leverage and introduce liquidity standards.

blocks.title: RBI's Basel III capital rules (guidelines of 2 May 2012)
rows: At least 7% of risk weighted assets on an ongoing basis
Includes Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 5.5% in India
At least 9% of risk weighted assets
Banks disclose the capital ratio computed under existing guidelines from the year ending 31 March 2013
Raised to 4.5% from 2% under Basel II
Risk-weighted capital requirement more than doubled
Extra cushion built in good times

blocks.title: Two more ideas
rows: Buying assets with borrowed money to multiply gains, hoping the asset earns more than the loan interest. It is risky, so Basel III **limits leverage**. Understand the concept; the numbers are less important.

If all depositors demand money together, a bank can collapse, as happened with **Lehman Brothers** whose failure triggered the 2008 recession. So banks must hold liquid assets (easily convertible to cash) at all times. In India this correlates with maintaining **CRR and SLR**.

blocks.title: Liquidity standards in the framework
rows: Liquidity Coverage Ratio - enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a **30-day** stress.
Net Stable Funding Ratio - stable funding over a **one-year** horizon.

blocks.title: Capital stack in India (top to bottom)
Basel I, II, III: what each one added
blocks.phrase: I = capital for credit, II = pillars for supervision and disclosure, III = liquidity and leverage after the crisis.
letters: More and better capital; leverage; liquidity

blocks.title: Basel III numbers for India
blocks.phrase: Seven core, nine total, five and a half common equity, two and a half buffer.
letters: Common Equity Tier 1 minimum in India

blocks.title: LCR versus NSFR
blocks.phrase: Liquidity Coverage is a month; Net Stable Funding is a year.

sections.title: Basel III in India: timeline and challenges

blocks.title: Key dates
items: RBI released Basel III capital regulation guidelines
RBI began implementing Basel III recommendations in India
Implementation of the norms postponed earlier to this year
Later pushed further; the study material says 'now till 2023'

blocks.title: Challenges in implementing Basel III
rows: Private banks can raise capital from markets, but public sector banks depend mostly on the Government. The Government decided to infuse ₹12,000 crore in PSBs, and more is needed later.
Norms need more sophisticated technology and management styles; upgrading both is costly and hurts profitability.
Banks must hold more liquid assets, which earn modest returns, lowering operating profit margin; it may also crowd out good private investment and slow growth.

blocks.title: Three headaches: C-T-L
blocks.phrase: Capital, Technology, Liquidity: the C-T-L headaches of Basel III.
letters: Capital: more of it, especially for PSBs
Liquidity crunch: lower returns, crowding out

sections.title: Deferral of the final Basel III standards to 2023

blocks.text: In view of the **coronavirus pandemic**, the implementation of Basel III standards was **deferred by one year** from 1 January 2022 to **1 January 2023**. The decision was taken by the Basel Committee's oversight body, the **Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS)**.

blocks.title: What moved by one year
rows: Basel III standards finalised in December 2017
Transitional arrangements for the output floor

blocks.title: Why these standards matter
blocks.text: These later standards were finalised to complement the initial set of Basel III standards. The deferral came from the BCBS and its GHOS; dates in India may differ, so read the latest RBI notice.

revision: Basel is in Switzerland and hosts the BIS; the BCBS (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision) frames the norms.
Basel accords aim to make sure banks have enough capital to meet obligations and absorb unexpected losses.
First Basel Concordat (1975) was about division of supervisory responsibilities among national authorities.
Basel I (1988): 8% of risk weighted assets, focused on credit risk, defined capital and risk weights.
RWA means assets weighted by risk; collateral-backed assets carry lower risk than unsecured personal loans.
Basel II (2004): minimum capital 8% (CAR in India), better risk management, and disclosure.
Basel II pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline.
Basel III (2010) came after the 2008 financial crisis; Lehman Brothers' collapse is the liquidity example.
RBI Basel III guidelines of 2 May 2012: Tier 1 at least 7%, total capital at least 9% of RWA.
Basel III raised common equity to 4.5% from 2% under Basel II; leverage is capped.
Liquid assets under Basel III correlate in India with CRR and SLR; LCR covers 30 days, NSFR one year.
RBI implemented Basel III from 1 April 2013; full implementation was postponed to 2019 and later.
Challenges: higher capital (PSBs lean on the Government), technology cost, and liquidity crunch.
Market risk is the risk of losses on on- and off-balance sheet positions due to market price movements.
Pandemic deferral by GHOS: Basel III standards of December 2017 moved to 1 January 2023; output floor to 1 January 2028.
